rules.title: Fair Chance in Housing Act (criminal-record screening limits)
rules.requirement: Housing providers may not put criminal-record questions on an application, or ask about criminal records orally or in writing, before making a conditional offer. Two exceptions apply: methamphetamine manufacture on federally assisted premises, and lifetime sex-offender registration. At no point may a provider evaluate arrests or charges without conviction, expunged, pardoned, vacated or nullified convictions, juvenile adjudications, or sealed records. After a conditional offer, a provider may consider only (1) convictions for listed serious crimes or lifetime-registration offenses and (2) indictable offenses within these lookbacks: 6 years for first degree, 4 years for second or third degree, 1 year for fourth degree. A conditional offer may be withdrawn only if the provider finds, by a preponderance of the evidence, that withdrawal is necessary to fulfill a substantial, legitimate and nondiscriminatory interest. The provider must first do an individualized assessment. A withdrawal requires a written notice that states specific reasons and offers a chance to appeal. The applicant may request the information relied on within 30 days, and the provider must supply it free within 10 days. Before accepting any application fee, the provider must disclose in writing whether criminal history is reviewed and that the applicant may submit evidence of inaccuracy or rehabilitation. Providers may not require drug or alcohol tests or ask for consent to obtain drug-treatment records. Discriminatory advertising and misuse of records are prohibited. Enforcement is only through the Division on Civil Rights, not the courts. Penalties are up to $1,000, $5,000 or $10,000 depending on prior violations, and the Director may order the application fee returned.
rules.key_value: Post-offer lookback: 6 yrs (1st degree), 4 yrs (2nd/3rd degree), 1 yr (4th degree); no limit for listed serious crimes or lifetime registration; records request within 30 days, provided free within 10 days; penalties up to $1,000 / $5,000 / $10,000; 14-day mediation window

rules.title: Residential rental application fee cap ($50, CPI-adjusted)
rules.requirement: A landlord or agent may not require an application or similar fee above $50 to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes. Starting January 1 of the year after enactment, the cap is adjusted each year by the CPI-U (New York-Northern New Jersey-Long Island, All Items), but only if the percent change is greater than zero. The Director of Consumer Affairs publishes the current limit. Penalties are up to $500 for a first offense, $750 for a second and $1,000 for each later offense. They are enforced in summary proceedings in the Special Civil Part on complaint of the Director or the Attorney General. The amount wrongfully charged is remitted to the applicant. The Director must adopt rules, including a mechanism for reporting violations.

rules.title: New Jersey Security Deposit Law
rules.requirement: A landlord may not collect a security deposit of more than 1.5 times one month's rent. Any pet deposit counts toward that cap. Prepaid rent held to secure future rent, including last month's rent, also counts as deposit. At lease inception the landlord may require at most the 1.5-month deposit plus first month's rent. Yearly increases may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. The deposit stays the tenant's property and must be held in trust without commingling. It must be kept in an interest-bearing account at an insured New Jersey institution; landlords holding deposits for 10 or more units may instead use an insured NJ money market fund. Interest belongs to the tenant. Within 30 days of receipt, and at each annual interest payment, the landlord must give written notice of the institution, amount, account type and interest rate. If notice or interest is not provided, the tenant may apply the deposit plus 7% annual interest to rent. Within 30 days after the tenancy ends, the landlord must return the deposit plus interest less deductions. Deductions are limited to damage beyond normal wear and tear and other money due under the lease, and must be itemized by registered or certified mail. If a tenant is displaced by fire, flood, condemnation or evacuation, return is due within 5 business days. A tenant may sue for double the amount wrongfully withheld plus costs and attorney's fees. A new owner is responsible for the deposit. Willful withholding from tenants on government assistance carries civil penalties of $500 to $2,000, and unlawful use of deposits is a disorderly persons offense.

rules.title: New Jersey Anti-Eviction Act (good cause eviction)
rules.requirement: A residential landlord may not evict a tenant or refuse to renew a lease, written or oral, without one of the statutory good causes. These are: nonpayment of rent; disorderly conduct; willful or grossly negligent damage; substantial breach of rules or lease covenants after a Notice to Cease; failure to pay a rent increase that is not unconscionable and complies with local ordinances; health and safety removal or illegal occupancy; permanent retirement from residential use; refusal of reasonable lease changes; habitual late payment; condominium or cooperative conversion; owner or buyer occupancy after conversion or in small buildings; end of employment-based tenancy; and certain drug, assault, theft and human-trafficking findings. Every cause except nonpayment requires a detailed written Notice to Quit, and some causes require a Notice to Cease first. Only a court judgment for possession and a warrant of removal executed by a court officer can remove a tenant; self-help eviction is illegal. Tenants evicted to correct an illegal occupancy are owed relocation assistance of six times monthly rent. Landlords who misuse an owner-occupancy or retirement eviction face treble damages, and a civil penalty of up to $10,000 applies to residential reuse within 5 years of a retirement or demolition eviction. Rooming and boarding house owners must follow the same causes and notices and give the County Welfare Board 3 working days' notice. In owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings, only a narrower list of causes applies, including holdover after lease expiry.
rules.key_value: Notice to Quit: 3 days (disorderly conduct, damage, end of employment, drug/assault/theft); 1 month (rules or lease breach, rent increase, lease changes, habitual late payment); 2 months (post-conversion or small-building owner/buyer occupancy); 3 months (health and safety removal); 18 months (retirement from residential use); 3 years (conversion). Relocation for illegal occupancy: 6x monthly rent.

rules.title: Foreclosure tenant protections (Foreclosure Fairness Act)
rules.requirement: Foreclosure alone is not grounds for eviction. A buyer of a foreclosed property who wants to occupy it as a primary residence must give a 90-day notice to quit. A tenant whose lease runs longer may not be evicted until the lease expires. Anyone acquiring a foreclosed property with residential rental units must, within 10 business days after the sale, notify tenants in English and Spanish that ownership has changed and that they need not move. In buildings with more than 10 units, the notice is posted in a prominent location instead. Foreclosing creditors must give the court-rule notice of tenant rights. Any monetary offer to induce a tenant to leave must come with the separate tenant notice and a five-day review period. Pressure tactics are prohibited, including misrepresenting rights, harassment, and unlawful or unconscionable rent increases.

coverage.summary: Applies to residential rental units in foreclosed properties. Month-to-month tenants and owner-occupied two- and three-family units are not exempt from the 90-day notice. In buildings with more than 10 units, posting replaces individual notices.
coverage.other_conditions: Triggered only by a foreclosure and the sale or transfer of the property.

rules.title: Reprisal (anti-retaliation) protections for tenants
rules.requirement: A landlord may not retaliate by eviction, substantial alteration of a lease or its terms, or refusal to renew a lease because a tenant exercised protected rights. Those rights are: (1) enforcing rights under the lease or State or local law; (2) making a good-faith complaint to a governmental authority about a health or safety violation, after first notifying the landlord in writing and allowing reasonable time to correct it; (3) organizing or belonging to a lawful organization, including a tenant organization; and (4) refusing lease changes made in retaliation. A tenant may sue for damages.

rules.title: Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act (conversion protected tenancy)
rules.requirement: When a building is converted to condominium, cooperative or fee-simple ownership, a qualifying tenant may obtain protected tenancy and may be protected from eviction for 40 years. Qualifying tenants are those aged 62 or older before the conversion recording date, permanently disabled tenants, and veterans with a 60% or higher service-connected disability. The tenant must have lived in the building at least one year before the recording date. Family income must not exceed three times the county average per-person income or $50,000, whichever is greater. The landlord or converter must notify tenants of the right to apply. Applications are generally due within 60 days. The Tenant Protection Act of 1992 extends similar protection to qualified tenants in qualified counties (currently only Hudson County).

rules.title: Bar on rent increases to cover condominium/cooperative conversion costs
rules.requirement: When a building is converted to condominium, cooperative or fee-simple ownership of units, rents may not be increased to cover costs resulting solely from the conversion. Increases to cover the cost of new services or amenities are still allowed. The bar applies to all tenants in the building, whether or not they qualify for protected tenancy as seniors or disabled persons.

rules.title: Law Against Discrimination: source of lawful income and other protected characteristics in rental
rules.requirement: The LAD bars refusing to rent, or discriminating in the terms of a rental, on the basis of race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, marital, civil union or domestic partnership status, familial status, affectional or sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, disability, nationality, or source of lawful income or source of lawful rent payment. For example, a landlord cannot deny a Section 8 voucher holder an apartment based solely on that source of income. Discriminatory advertising is prohibited. A landlord may still refuse to rent for insufficient income, an oversized family, occupancy that would violate zoning, or poor credit history. Complaints may be filed free with the Division on Civil Rights within 180 days, or in Superior Court within two years. Penalties are up to $10,000 for a first offense.

rules.title: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act
rules.requirement: It is unlawful, and a violation of the New Jersey Antitrust Act, for: (a) a rental property owner or its agent to pay for, subscribe to or contract for the services of a coordinator; (b) a coordinator to facilitate an agreement among rental property owners that restricts competition, including by performing a coordinating function; (c) two or more persons to engage in or facilitate parallel pricing coordination; (d) a coordinator's agent to engage in parallel pricing coordination; or (e) any person to perform a coordinating function. A coordinating function is algorithmic or automated rent-setting that uses competitively sensitive nonpublic information of two or more owners, or of any other owner, or that applies the same algorithm to set or recommend rents, lease terms or occupancy for two or more owners. Antitrust Act remedies (C.56:9-6 to 9-17) apply. The Attorney General must set up a complaint location and may adopt rules. Municipalities may not enact conflicting ordinances.
rules.key_value: Effective July 1, 2027; violations are New Jersey Antitrust Act violations; conflicting municipal ordinances prohibited

coverage.landlord_size_condition: Applies to any rental property owner owning one or more rental residential dwelling units; controlled entities are treated as a single owner.
coverage.summary: Covers residential dwelling units (houses, apartments, accessory units, other primary residences) in New Jersey. Inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or correctional facilities are excluded.
coverage.other_conditions: The following are not a coordinating function: research, statistical or testing use not used to set rents; free public rent estimates; equal-terms brokerage listing databases that do not set or recommend rents; government affordability controls. Spreadsheets without AI that require human analysis, and databases that only query unprocessed data, are not algorithmic devices.

rules.exemptions: Research or testing uses, free public rent estimates, equal-terms brokerage databases, and government affordability controls are not coordinating functions. Spreadsheets without AI that require human analysis and databases that only query unprocessed data are not algorithmic devices. Inpatient medical, licensed long-term care and correctional facilities are excluded.

Jersey City (§ 218-12, Ord. 25-057/25-076) and Hoboken (§ 158-2) already have algorithmic rent-fixing bans with different definitions, penalties and private enforcement. DX16 describes coordinators as using data 'from multiple' owners, but the statutory definition also covers an owner performing a coordinating function for its own benefit; the statute controls.

also_supported_by.quoted_span: The FAIR Act takes effect on July 1, 2027, providing affected property owners, managers, and software providers time to review and, if necessary, modify their pricing practices before the law becomes effective.

The FAIR Act prohibits residential rental property owners from using algorithmic revenue management software that collects or processes competitors' nonpublic leasing information to set or recommend rental prices.
